name: Mérida & Chichén Itzá
tagline: The Maya heartland: a great pyramid on the plain, a white colonial city of haciendas and cochinita pibil, and limestone cenotes to swim in between them.
highlight: El Castillo at Chichén Itzá at opening, and a swim in a cenote before lunch.
shortDescription: Yucatán's cultural centre, with the New Wonder of Chichén Itzá, the Puuc ruins of Uxmal, Valladolid's convents and cenotes, and Mérida, a graceful colonial city with the best food on the peninsula.
metaDescription: A Mérida and Chichén Itzá travel guide: El Castillo, Uxmal, Ek Balam, cenotes, Valladolid, Mérida's cathedral and Paseo de Montejo, Yucatecan food, when to go and a three-day plan.
nearestAirport: Mérida Manuel Crescencio Rejón (MID), about 20 minutes
knownFor: Chichén Itzá, Uxmal, cenotes, Yucatecan cuisine, colonial Mérida
goodFor: Maya archaeology, cenotes, food, colonial architecture

image.alt: El Castillo, the stepped pyramid of Chichén Itzá, on its plaza under a blue sky

intro: The Yucatán Peninsula is a flat limestone plain without rivers, where the ancient Maya built cities around natural sinkholes called cenotes, which supplied their water. Chichén Itzá, the most famous, flourished from about 800 to 1200 CE, and its pyramid, El Castillo, is aligned so that at the equinoxes the shadow of a serpent appears to slither down its staircase. It is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World and a UNESCO site.

Mérida, the state capital, was founded by the Spanish in 1542 on the site of a Maya city, and it is the cultural centre of the peninsula: a city of pastel colonial houses, plazas, a large cathedral built from Maya temple stones, and the grand mansions of the henequen boom on Paseo de Montejo. It is warm, safe and relaxed, and the best food base in Yucatán.

The region between them is rich in sights. Uxmal, south of Mérida, is a masterpiece of Puuc-style architecture. Valladolid is a colourful colonial town with a cenote in its centre, and Ek Balam has a climbable pyramid with a well-preserved stucco facade. Together, they make an easy loop of three or four days.

whyVisit.intro: This is the best place in Mexico to see the Maya world, and to eat the food of the peninsula.

points.title: Chichén Itzá
points.text: The pyramid of Kukulcán, the great ball court, the Temple of the Warriors and the sacred cenote are among the greatest monuments of Mesoamerica.

points.title: Uxmal
points.text: A quieter, more elegant Puuc city with the Pyramid of the Magician and the Governor's Palace, and richly carved facades.

points.title: Cenotes
points.text: Sinkholes with clear turquoise water, some in caves with stalactites and some open to the sky, are ideal for swimming.

points.title: Mérida
points.text: A walkable colonial city with Sunday markets, free concerts in the plaza, and a lively food scene.

points.title: Yucatecan food
points.text: Cochinita pibil, sopa de lima, papadzules and panuchos are unlike anything else in Mexico.

attractionsIntro: Chichén Itzá needs half a day, Uxmal another half, and Mérida a full day.

attractions.name: Chichén Itzá
attractions.text: A vast Maya and Toltec-influenced city with El Castillo, the Great Ball Court, the Temple of the Warriors, the Observatory (El Caracol) and the Sacred Cenote. The pyramid can no longer be climbed.
attractions.tip: Arrive at opening, and consider visiting in the afternoon, when the crowds thin.

attractions.name: Uxmal
attractions.text: A Puuc-style Maya city with the Pyramid of the Magician, the Nunnery Quadrangle and the Governor's Palace, decorated with intricate mosaic stonework and rain-god masks.
attractions.tip: Stay for the evening light and sound show if it is running.

attractions.name: Mérida's Plaza Grande and Cathedral

image.alt: The 16th-century cathedral of Mérida on the Plaza Grande

attractions.text: The main square, with the 16th-century cathedral, one of the oldest in the Americas, the Governor's Palace with murals of Maya history, and the Casa de Montejo.
attractions.tip: Free concerts and dances take place most evenings.

attractions.name: Paseo de Montejo
attractions.text: A grand boulevard modelled on the Champs-Élysées, lined with mansions built by henequen barons, now museums, banks and restaurants. The Gran Museo del Mundo Maya is nearby.
attractions.tip: Go on a Sunday, when the road is closed to traffic.

attractions.name: Valladolid and Cenote Zací

image.file: File:Cenote Zaci, Valladolid de Yucatan, Julio 2012 01.jpg
image.alt: A swimmer in Cenote Zací, a cenote in the centre of Valladolid

attractions.text: A small colonial town of pastel houses and a Franciscan convent, with a large open cenote a few blocks from the main square.
attractions.tip: A good lunch stop between Mérida and Chichén Itzá.

attractions.name: Ek Balam

image.alt: The main pyramid and stucco facade at the Maya site of Ek Balam

attractions.text: A smaller Maya city north of Valladolid with a large acropolis, a stucco-sculpted tomb entrance and few visitors.

attractions.name: Haciendas and Celestún
attractions.text: Restored henequen haciendas offer lunch and swimming, and the Celestún estuary, 90 minutes west, is a flamingo reserve.
attractions.tip: Flamingos are best seen from November to March.

thingsToDoIntro: A loop through the heart of Yucatán combines ruins, swimming and eating.

thingsToDo.title: See Chichén Itzá early
thingsToDo.text: Go at opening for cooler temperatures, softer light and smaller crowds.
thingsToDo.tip: Hire a licensed guide at the gate, or download an audio guide.

thingsToDo.title: Swim in a cenote
thingsToDo.text: Cenote Ik Kil, Suytun and Zací are among many that can be visited.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring a towel and a dry bag, and rinse off first.

thingsToDo.title: Eat cochinita pibil
thingsToDo.text: Try it in a Mérida market, on a taco, with habanero salsa and pickled onions.
thingsToDo.tip: Ask for it 'con todo' for the works.

thingsToDo.title: Spend a Sunday in Mérida
thingsToDo.text: Paseo de Montejo is closed to cars, and the plaza hosts a market, music and dance.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Uxmal and hacienda
thingsToDo.text: Combine the ruins with a hacienda lunch on the Puuc route.
thingsToDo.tip: Hire a driver for the day.

thingsToDo.title: Try a traditional Maya ceremony or workshop
thingsToDo.text: Local cooperatives offer cooking, weaving and honey-tasting, run by Maya families.

foodIntro: Yucatecan cuisine is distinct from the rest of Mexico, with Maya, Spanish, Caribbean and Lebanese influences and its own spices.

foods.name: Cochinita pibil
foods.text: Pork marinated in sour orange and achiote, wrapped in banana leaves and slow-cooked.

foods.name: Sopa de lima
foods.text: A chicken and tortilla soup flavoured with a local sour lime.

foods.name: Papadzules and panuchos
foods.text: Egg-filled tortillas in pumpkin-seed sauce, and fried tortillas stuffed with black beans and topped with turkey.

foods.name: Poc chuc and lechón al horno
foods.text: Grilled marinated pork and roast suckling pig, both served with pickles and tortillas.

foods.name: Habanero salsa and xnipec
foods.text: Fiery chile sauces on every table, to be used sparingly.

foods.name: Marquesitas and helado
foods.text: Crisp rolled crepes filled with cheese and Nutella, and ice cream, sold on the Mérida plazas.

accommodation.intro: Mérida is the best base, and staying near Chichén Itzá lets you see it at opening.

areas.name: Mérida centro
areas.text: Boutique hotels in restored colonial houses with courtyards and pools, near the plazas.

areas.name: Valladolid
areas.text: Small hotels and guesthouses, 45 minutes from Chichén Itzá and close to several cenotes.

areas.name: Haciendas
areas.text: Restored haciendas outside Mérida offer pools, gardens and history.

gettingThere.intro: Mérida has an airport, and buses and the Tren Maya link it to the rest of the peninsula.

options.text: Direct flights from Mexico City, Cancún and several US cities.
options.detail: Taxis and Uber run into the city.

options.text: ADO buses take about 4 hours from Cancún and 5 from Tulum. Chichén Itzá is on the way.
A tourist rail connection between Mérida, Cancún and other destinations.

gettingAround.intro: Mérida is walkable, and tours, colectivos and hire cars cover the region.

options.text: The centre is compact. Taxis and Uber are cheap.
Useful for Uxmal, cenotes and haciendas. Roads are flat and straight, with speed bumps in villages.
Shared vans go to Chichén Itzá, Valladolid and the cenotes.

bestTime.headline: November–March
bestTime.summary: Yucatán is hot and humid for much of the year. The dry winter months are the most comfortable, and summer brings extreme heat and storms.

seasons.text: Warm, dry and sunny, with pleasant nights.
Hot, up to 38°C, and dry. Go early for the ruins.
Hot, humid and rainy, with hurricane risk. Cheaper and green.
Humid at first, and pleasant by November.

bestTime.avoid: Midday in April to September, and the spring equinox at Chichén Itzá if you want quiet.

itinerary.title: Three days in Yucatán
itinerary.intro: Mérida on the first day, Uxmal on the second, Chichén Itzá and Valladolid on the third. Assumes a hire car or a driver.

days.title: Mérida
days.morning: The Plaza Grande, the cathedral and the markets.
days.afternoon: Paseo de Montejo and the Gran Museo del Mundo Maya.
days.evening: Cochinita pibil and a plaza concert.

days.title: Uxmal and a hacienda
days.afternoon: Lunch at a hacienda and a swim.

days.title: Chichén Itzá and Valladolid
days.summary: The great pyramid and a cenote.
days.afternoon: A swim in a cenote and lunch in Valladolid.
days.evening: Return to Mérida or continue to Tulum.

tipsIntro: Yucatán is hot and flat, and a few tips help.
tips: Go to Chichén Itzá at opening, and bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
Use biodegradable sunscreen or none in cenotes, and rinse before swimming.
Carry small pesos for entry fees, colectivos and vendors.
Ask before you photograph Maya people, and buy crafts directly.
Do not climb pyramids where it is forbidden. Rules at smaller sites change, so check the signs and ask the guards.
Drive carefully. Speed bumps (topes) appear without warning.
Book a table on Sunday evenings in Mérida.

faq.q: Can I climb the pyramid at Chichén Itzá?
faq.a: No. Climbing El Castillo has been prohibited since 2006. Rules for climbing at other sites change and are often restricted, so check on arrival.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Yucatán?
faq.a: Three or four for Mérida, Uxmal and Chichén Itzá, and more to add Valladolid, Ek Balam and the coast.
It is widely regarded as one of the safest cities in Mexico. Normal precautions apply.
A natural sinkhole in limestone that exposes groundwater. The Maya regarded them as sacred and used them as water sources.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit?
faq.a: November to March for the ruins. Summer is very hot, humid and rainy.

faq.q: Can I visit Chichén Itzá as a day trip from Cancún?
faq.a: Yes, but it is about 2.5 hours each way. Staying near the site or in Valladolid lets you arrive at opening.
